name: Sigmoid
seoDesc: Sigmoid: work out your result from the output of sigmoid function, σ. A free math calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary:
The Sigmoid calculator returns your result from the field on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below.

Think of it as a shortcut for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Sigmoid calculator work?
sections.html:
The Sigmoid calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the output of sigmoid function, σ(x).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html: • A plain number with no unit attached.

sections.title: The formula behind the Sigmoid calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Finite real input, x=the natural log of (-output of sigmoid function, σ(x) ÷ (output of sigmoid function, σ(x) − 1))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
The form opens with a complete set of values: Finite real input, x = 0. Straight away the calculator returns Output of sigmoid function, σ(x) = 0.5.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Output of sigmoid function, σ(x) = 0.5 should be roughly the size you expected from Finite real input, x = 0.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Sigmoid calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the output of sigmoid function, σ — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Sigmoid calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — output of sigmoid function, σ for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Sigmoid calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the output of sigmoid function, σ, which is a single field. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Output of sigmoid function, σ(x) = 0.5. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Sigmoid calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
